name: Vera Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do the office for a family plumbing and heating firm, six engineers and the owner, Pete. I answer the phones, book the boiler services into the big diary, send out the invoices and file the gas safety certificates in the cabinets. We still use a paper diary alongside the computer, because Pete likes to flick through it, and so do I. I've been there two years and I'm still getting the hang of the accounts package.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best and worst of it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best is when an old lady rings in a panic because her heating's off in January, and I can get Marek round by four. You feel useful. The worst is the accounts software, it's always updating and moving buttons, and I end up ringing Pete's daughter-in-law to ask where things went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, all that fuss for nothing. At work I'd probably make a joke to Pete about it. I don't really post online, so I'd just mention it to my sister.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be relieved, but not completely. Danny, Pete's son, keeps saying we should get an online booking system so customers book themselves. Even if AI turns out to be hype, that sort of thing still comes in, and that's half my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and try to stay useful. I'd probably put a bit more aside, because I've only got about two months saved and the rent on my flat goes up in the spring. I wouldn't go near any AI stuff, I've never used it and I don't see why I'd start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, if I'm honest. It's like when a car keeps making a small noise and you hope it's nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the booking system is half your job. Have they actually decided anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. Danny brings it up at the Christmas do every year, and Pete says not while he's alive. But Pete's sixty-four, and Danny's going to run the firm one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Danny got the booking system, what would that mean for your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer hours, probably. I'm full-time now, but if customers book online, the firm might keep me three days a week. Three days wouldn't cover my rent. I'd need something else on top.

say: I'd say all that **fuss was for nothing**, and joke about it with Pete.
I'd only mention it to my **sister**, because I don't post online.
think: An **online booking system** could still come in and take half my job.
When **Pete retires**, his son Danny is likely to bring it in.
do: Keep **staying useful** at the firm and avoid AI tools completely.
Put more aside, since I've only **two months saved** and rent rises in spring.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a small car noise you hope is **nothing**.
S0.quote: I'm full-time now, but if customers book online, the firm might keep me three days a week. Three days wouldn't cover my rent.
fieldNote: Her threat in a calm world is a **booking website**, not AI itself.
Job security hangs on the **owner's age** and his son's plans.
She **avoids new tools** and would rather wait than learn.

steps.text: Keep running the phones and paper diary for the engineers
Save extra each month before the spring rent rise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame and that people still want to talk to a person when their boiler's broken. That's what I'd tell anyone who asked. I'd say small firms like ours will be the last to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, though, I think I'm in trouble. Booking, invoicing, answering customers, that's literally what I do all day. If my boss's son can buy a program that does booking, invoices and the phone, I'm the cost he cuts. And I'm not good with computers, so I can't even be the one who runs it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably wait and see what Danny does first, because I don't want to jump at shadows. If he brings it in, I'd look for another office job nearby, maybe at the vets or the doctors' surgery. I'd stop the gym and the takeaways straight away so the savings last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A bit sick, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. Is that really what you'd do, or what you'd like to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. It's what I'd like to do. I know I should probably learn the computer stuff, but every time I try, I get flustered and feel stupid, so I put it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister, Jun. She's a teaching assistant and she's much better with this stuff. She'd tell me to do a course, and I'd say yes and then not do it, probably.

say: I'd say people still want a **real person** when their boiler breaks.
I'd tell people **small firms** like ours will be the last to change.
think: Booking, invoicing and answering customers are **exactly my job**.
I'm not good with computers, so I can't be the one who **runs the program**.
do: **Wait and see** what Danny does before jumping at shadows.
Look for **office work** at the vets or doctors' surgery if the program arrives.
Stop the **gym and takeaways** straight away so savings last.
S1.quote: If my boss's son can buy a program that does booking, invoices and the phone, I'm the cost he cuts.
fieldNote: She knows her tasks match the card but plans to **wait and see**.
Admits **avoidance**: she gets flustered with computers and puts off learning.
Relies on her **sister** for advice she says she won't follow.

steps.text: Wait to see if Danny buys a booking program
Apply for office jobs at the vets or doctors' surgery
Cancel the gym and stop takeaways

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and somebody should stop it. I'm not political, but I'd say the government has to do something for people like me. Pete would say plumbers will always be needed, and he'd be right for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm finished in the office. If AI can do anything I can do at a desk, Danny won't need me at all by 2028. I've got no degree, two months saved, and I've never even opened one of those chat programs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. Maybe I'd ask Pete if I could train up on the tools, helping the lads on site, because your card says robots come later. I'd move back in with my mum if I had to, to save the rent. That's about as far as I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I feel like I'm standing on the platform watching the train leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned training on the tools. Is that realistic for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I'm not afraid of getting dirty, and Marek says the job is half common sense. But I'm twenty-seven and I'd be starting at the bottom on a lad's wage, and in three years the robots come for that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would moving back in with your mum mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd mean my old bedroom with the pink wallpaper, which I'd hate. But Mum would love it, and it'd mean I wasn't paying rent while I worked out what to do. She'd feed me, and I'd do her shopping.

say: I'd say it's **frightening** and the government should **do something**.
I'd agree with Pete that **plumbers** will be needed for a few years.
think: I'm **finished** in the office, because Danny won't need me by 2028.
With **no degree** and two months saved, I've no fallback.
do: Ask Pete about training as a **plumber's mate** on site.
Move back in with **Mum** to stop paying rent.
feel: **Alarmed**, like watching the **train leave** from the platform.
S2.quote: I'm twenty-seven and I'd be starting at the bottom on a lad's wage, and in three years the robots come for that too.
fieldNote: She has **no real plan**, just a vague idea of site work.
Moving home to **her mum** is the one solid move she names.
She sees the **robot delay** but notes it only buys three years.

steps.text: Ask Pete about training as a plumber's mate
Move back in with Mum to save the rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, it's scary, but at least there's some warning. I'd tell people at the firm that we'd better all think about it. I'd probably sign a petition if my sister sent me one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years helps a bit, but not much for someone like me. I'm slow to change, I know that. I'd probably spend the first two years telling myself it's not really coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job as long as Pete keeps me, and try to save, maybe get to four months. My sister would push me to do an evening course in something hands-on, maybe care work or hairdressing. I'd probably sign up, and I'd like to think I'd stick with it this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed, just slower. Like the same bad news with a longer fuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd spend two years telling yourself it's not coming. What would break that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the day Danny sits me down. If he says, we're getting the system, you're down to three days, then I'd move. I'm the sort of person who needs the shock before I do anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you did do care work, how would that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be all right at it, I think. I'm good with the old ladies on the phone, and I looked after Nan when she was ill. It'd be less money, but at least it's people, not screens.

say: I'd say it's **scary**, but at least there's some **warning**.
I'd tell people at the firm we'd all better **think about it**.
think: Five years helps, but I'm **slow to change** and know it.
I'd spend two years **telling myself** it's not really coming.
do: Stay at the firm and save toward **four months**.
Sign up for an **evening course** in care work, pushed by my sister.
Move only when **Danny** cuts my hours.
S3.quote: I'm the sort of person who needs the shock before I do anything.
fieldNote: Extra time barely helps, because she expects to **delay** acting.
Care work fits her **phone manner** and her past caring for her nan.
Her trigger is the moment her **hours are cut**, not the news itself.

steps.text: Save toward four months of rent and bills
Sign up for an evening course in care work
Wait until Danny cuts her hours before changing job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long way off, and loads can happen in ten years. That's what I'd say to anyone, and I'd mostly believe it. I'd probably not talk about it much at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels like enough time for me to be dragged along slowly. I'd still be in the office for a while, and by the time it comes, I'd hope I'd have moved into something else. But I know myself, and I'd leave it late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at the firm for now. In a few years I'd probably do the care course my sister keeps mentioning, or ask Pete about the tools. I'd keep saving and maybe, eventually, try one of those AI programs, if someone showed me in person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not sick like the fast one. More of a low hum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe, eventually. What would make you try an AI program?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jun sitting next to me with a cup of tea, showing me slowly. Not a video, not a manual. I learn from people, not from screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you see yourself in the office at thirty-five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to, honestly, but I don't think the office will be there in the same way. Maybe I'd be the one who rings the customers back when the computer gets it wrong. Someone has to say sorry properly.

say: I'd say ten years is **a long way off** and loads can happen.
I'd mostly **not talk** about it at all.
think: Ten years is enough time to be **dragged along** slowly.
I know myself, and I'd **leave it late**.
do: Keep going at the firm and keep **saving** each month.
Do the **care course** or ask Pete about the tools in a few years.
Try an **AI program** only if my sister shows me in person.
feel: **Anxious**, but a **low hum** rather than sick.
S4.quote: I'd be the one who rings the customers back when the computer gets it wrong. Someone has to say sorry properly.
fieldNote: Ten years gives her **room** but she expects to waste some of it.
She **learns from people**, not screens, which shapes any training.
Hopes for a niche as the **human voice** when software fails.

steps.text: Keep booking boiler services at the firm for now
Take the care course in a few years
Learn an AI program with Jun's help at home

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. No time, no plan, and I'd be back in my pink bedroom at my mum's. What would help is someone actually showing me what to do, in person, and a bit of money while I retrain, because I can't afford to stop earning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how embarrassing it is to be bad at computers when you're my age. Everyone assumes young people are good at computers. I'm not, and that makes all of this harder.

headlineQuote: Everyone assumes young people are good at computers. I'm not, and that makes all of this harder.
portrait: Vera runs the **phones and paper diary** for a family plumbing and heating firm.
She's **pragmatic**, not political, and leans on her sister Jun for advice.
She **avoids technology**, gets flustered by software and has never used AI.
Even in the mildest world she fears the owner's son's **booking system**.
In fast scenarios she has **no plan** beyond moving back in with her mum.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time and she has no plan.
whatWouldHelp: Someone teaching her **in person**, plus some **money** while retraining.
